name: Orris Hour
description: A fictional fragrance development and launch presentation.

slides.title: Orris Hour
items: EAU DE PARFUM
Bitter orange, iris and cedar

slides.title: The brief
items: An iris for the hour before dusk.
The studio wanted the cool, powdery impression of iris to arrive slowly. An orange-peel opening gives the wearer a distinct first impression, then recedes as the floral body settles.
The sample was assessed on paper at application, at thirty minutes and again after four hours. Each reading answers a different question about the same composition.

slides.title: The peel
items: At application
The perfumer chose the bitterness of the rind as the opening impression. A sweeter orange trial lingered into the middle and made the iris harder to pick out.
The selected trial has a bright first minute and a clean exit. Its role is to mark the start of the wear, leaving space for the powdery centre.

slides.title: Three readings on paper
items: Relative impression in the studio trial, scored from 0 to 5.
Orange falls from five to one by the second reading. Iris reaches its highest score at thirty minutes, then gives way to cedar. The last strip still carries a faint floral impression.

slides.title: The heart
items: Thirty minutes
“I noticed the iris when I picked the strip up again. The orange had gone, but I could still remember where it had been.”
From the studio’s second blotter reading

slides.title: A bottle for the hand
items: Orris Hour
50 mL
The broad base sits flat on a dressing table. Rounded shoulders leave a smooth edge where the palm rests, and a short stopper keeps the silhouette low.
The pale label leaves the fill line visible on both sides. A single dark cap gives the bottle a clear outline against the light paper carton.

slides.title: At the counter
items: One strip for now. One for later.
A guest smells the first strip at the counter. The second goes into a dated paper sleeve, with the time written on its flap so the guest can revisit the scent that afternoon.
The tester stays beside the strips. Take-home samples sit farther along the counter, where the guest can stop and speak to the host.

slides.title: The first filling
items: 240 bottles
180 for the opening release
The counter receives three trays of sixty. Staff open one tray at a time so unopened stock remains in its carton.
48 for partner shops
Four stockists receive twelve bottles each, with enough blotters for two weekends of sampling.
12 held by the studio
The studio keeps twelve for photography, display replacements and comparisons with the next filling.

slides.title: Two trial strips
items: Trial A
A sweeter orange opening stayed prominent at thirty minutes. Two readers described the middle as soft, but neither named the iris until the final reading.
Trial B
The leaner peel note cleared sooner. Both readers picked out the iris at the second reading. The studio chose this version for the first filling.

slides.title: The wrap
items: A carton the colour of the blotter
The name sits on the front face. The side panel carries the volume and composition details. A narrow plum fold is visible only when the top flap opens.
The first paper mock-up was folded around a filled bottle. The studio widened the base tuck so the carton could stand square on the counter.

slides.title: The studio appointment
items: A twenty-minute visit
The host opens with the fresh strip and offers a second strip prepared half an hour earlier. Smelling them together makes the change in emphasis easy to follow in the guest’s own description.
At the end of the visit, the guest selects a sample and writes down the time. The studio asks for one observation after the final reading that evening.

slides.title: Four hours later
items: By evening, cedar is the clearest note on the strip. The iris sits close to it, and the orange has disappeared.
The guest takes home the whole progression in a single bottle. The card in the carton gives the three reading times for a second wear.
